title: Water from a drilled well with no power
summary: Four ways to get water out of a drilled well when the power is off: a narrow well bucket on a rope, a hand pump hung in the casing beside the submersible, a generator big enough to start the submersible, or a DC pump on solar. The dangers are the mains wiring at the well head, a generator backfeeding the house, heavy pipe dropping down the well, and bad air in pits and dug wells.

materials.item: Pipe for the bucket body, about 1.2 m long, narrower than the clear gap down your casing (Gwinn used drainpipe)
Foot valve or check valve for the bottom, or a wooden plug, rubber ball and bolt as the valve
Bolts, washers and nuts for the cross-bolt and valve
Weight about 2 kg (window weight or steel bar) hung inside the top
Rope, nylon if you can (Alberta recommends nylon for pump safety ropes), longer than the depth to water, plus a few metres
Plain unscented household bleach, to clean the bucket and rope before use (1 part to 20 parts water)
Deep-well hand pump made to fit beside a submersible (Simple Pump, Bison)
Generator with an output that matches the pump's voltage label, sized from the table in the notes, and a transfer switch

steps.text: Find your well record (the well contractor's report) for casing size, depth and resting water level (Health Canada well treatment). The water level, not the well depth, sets how much rope or pipe you need.
Switch off and lock off the well pump's breaker, tape a note on it, then lift the well cap (Simple Pump install).
steps.warn: Wires may be exposed once the cap is off, and working with water near electricity risks shock (Health Canada well treatment). Never open a cap with the pump powered. If the well head is in a pit or pump house, don't climb in: gas can build up there (CDC well disinfection; EFP water wells).

steps.text: Shine a strong light or reflect the sun down the casing with a mirror and look for a clear path beside the drop pipe and cable, and for the water shining (Simple Pump install).

Build the bucket: a tube with a one-way valve in the bottom that opens as it sinks and closes as you lift (Solinst bailer), a cross-bolt near the top, and an optional weight hung from the cross-bolt to make it heavier so it fills faster (Gwinn 1976).

Wash the bucket and rope in 1 part plain unscented bleach to 20 parts water (about 250 mL in 5 L), then rinse every trace of it off before they go in (Simple Pump install; Health Canada well treatment). Never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or other cleaners: it makes toxic gas ([Chemicals](#browse/hazards/chemical)). Keep both off the ground from now on.
Tie the rope to the bucket with a bowline (Solinst bailer). Tie the other end to the casing or a post before you start, so the whole rope can't follow it down.
steps.warn: Anything that falls down the well can foul the pump: Goulds warns that even loose electrical tape can block its suction (Goulds IM117). Fishing a bucket out is slow, blind work.

steps.text: Lower it slowly until you hear it hit the water, give a little more slack, and wait for the gurgle as it fills (Gwinn 1976). Pull it up steadily, hand over hand.
Empty it by standing it in your pail and setting it down gently so the valve bolt pushes the valve open (Gwinn 1976). Put the well cap back between draws.
For a hand pump beside the submersible, follow the maker's manual with two people, power locked off, and a clamp holding the pipe string at every joint (Simple Pump install).
steps.warn: Pipes can drop down the well during assembly. At 41 m (135 ft) the string weighs about 34 kg. The install also disconnects and reconnects the pump's wiring under the cap, and Simple Pump says not to attempt that without training or experience (Simple Pump install).

steps.text: For the generator, check the pump's horsepower and whether it is a 2-wire or 3-wire motor against the generator sizes in the notes (Goulds IM117; Franklin AIM 60 Hz). Have it connected only through a transfer device or switch, so the generator can't feed back into the utility lines (ESA generators; Franklin AIM 60 Hz).
steps.warn: Never feed the house by plugging the generator into a wall outlet: backfeed can electrocute line workers and neighbours on the same transformer (CPSC 5123). The connection is mains-voltage work for someone who has done it. Treat the wiring as live: the grid can come back (ESA Flash 25-15-FL).

steps.text: Run the generator outdoors at least 6 m (20 ft) from buildings (Health Canada CO). Start it before switching the pump on, and switch the pump off before stopping it (Goulds IM117).
steps.warn: Never run a generator indoors, in a garage or shed (Health Canada CO), or in a well house: in a closed space CO reaches deadly levels within minutes (CPSC 5123).

steps.text: If you must pull the submersible, first make sure the pump's breaker is off and locked off again (Simple Pump install). Use two people, as Simple Pump does for its pipe string (Simple Pump install), and keep any safety rope tied off at the casing (Alberta submersible pumps). Lift by the pipe, never the cable (Goulds IM117).
steps.warn: The pipe comes up full of water and is heavier than it looks. Keep hands clear of the casing edge as it slides.

steps.text: Treat the water you draw as unsafe until a test shows otherwise: Health Canada's advice for a contaminated well is a rolling boil for 1 minute or another safe water source (Health Canada well treatment).

notes:
## What you're working with
A drilled well is a steel or plastic pipe (the casing), usually 10 to 20 cm (4 to 8 in) across and often 30 to 60 m (100 to 200 ft) deep; a dug well is 60 to 120 cm (24 to 48 in) wide and usually 3 to 9 m (10 to 30 ft) deep (GNB wells). The submersible pump hangs near the bottom on a drop pipe, its cable taped to the pipe (Goulds IM117). In many wells the pipe leaves the casing underground, below frost depth, through a pitless adapter (Wisconsin DG-022), so the top of the casing is just a cap.

Your well record (driller's report) gives the depth, casing size and resting (static) water level (Health Canada well treatment).

| Way | Power | Pump stays in? | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Well bucket (bailer) | None | Only if there's room beside the pipe | A few pails a day |
| Hand pump in the casing | None (12/24 V option) | Yes, beside it in 10 cm (4 in) or wider casing | Daily water for a household |
| Generator on the submersible | Fuel | Yes | Filling tanks fast while fuel lasts |
| DC pump on solar | Sun | Beside it (motorised hand pump) or instead of it | Long-term water once set up |

## The well bucket
A bailer is a tube with a one-way valve in its bottom: lowering it into the water pushes the valve open so it fills, and lifting it closes the valve and holds the water (Solinst bailer). Clifford Gwinn's 1976 design used about 1.2 m (4 ft) of 10 cm (4 in) drainpipe with a wooden plug in the bottom, a rubber ball sliding on a bolt as the valve, an optional 2.3 kg (5 lb) window weight to make it heavier so it fills faster, and it held about 11 L (3 US gal) a trip (Gwinn 1976). A ready-made foot valve or check valve glued into the bottom does the same job.

- **Size it to the gap, not the casing.** Most submersible pumps are made for casing at least 10 cm (4 in) inside, with a few for 7.5 cm (3 in) (Alberta submersible pumps), so with a pump in the well the clear space beside it can be small. Simple Pump needs a clear 41 to 64 mm (1.6 to 2.5 in) for its pipe (Simple Pump install). Measure the clear gap you can see and make the bucket narrower than it, with room to spare. A full 10 cm × 1.2 m tube is about 10 kg of water to haul each trip.
- **Weight it.** A weight hung from a cross-bolt near the top makes it heavier so it fills faster (Gwinn 1976).
- **Emptying:** stand it in your pail and set it down gently so the valve bolt pushes the valve open, or run a thin wire from the top cross-bolt to the valve bolt and pull it to open the valve (Gwinn 1976).
- **Keep it clean.** It touches your drinking water: wash it and the rope in 1 part plain unscented bleach to 20 parts water first, as Simple Pump does with its parts, and rinse every trace off (Simple Pump install; Health Canada well treatment). Never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or other cleaners ([Chemicals](#browse/hazards/chemical)). Keep both off the ground (Practica rope pump).

## Don't lose it down the well
- Tie the bucket on with a bowline (Solinst bailer), using nylon rope (Alberta recommends nylon for pump safety ropes), and tie the other end to the casing or a post before the first lowering, the way installers tie a pump's nylon safety rope off at the top of the casing (Alberta submersible pumps).
- Keep children and visitors well away from the open well head (Flotec pitcher pump).
- If the submersible and its pipe are still in the well, the bucket has to pass the pitless fitting, the cable and any centring guides. Simple Pump's hand-pump pipe needs a clear 41 to 64 mm (1.6 to 2.5 in) gap past the pitless adapter, and centring guides can block it (Simple Pump install). If you can't see a clear path, don't try.
- Look before you lower: shine a strong light, or reflect the sun with a mirror, down the casing. In a straight well you can see the water shine as deep as 60 m (200 ft) (Simple Pump install).
- Anything that falls in can foul the pump. Goulds warns that electrical tape coming loose off the drop pipe will block the pump's suction if it falls down the well (Goulds IM117).

## A hand pump beside the submersible
Deep-well hand pumps hang their own small pipe and cylinder in the casing next to the electric pump's drop pipe. Simple Pump fits alongside a submersible in 10 cm (4 in) or wider casing and is rated to a 99 m (325 ft) static water level; it can be a do-it-yourself job on pitless-adapter wells for someone comfortable with both plumbing and electrical wiring, and a pump contractor is advised where the pipe goes up through the cap (Simple Pump; Simple Pump install). The wiring is the dangerous part: the manual says not to attempt it without training or experience (Simple Pump install). Bison says its hand pumps can also go in beside an existing submersible (Bison FAQ).

What the install manual insists on (Simple Pump install):
- The submersible's power is locked off with a note on the breaker, because its wiring under the cap is disconnected and reconnected through the new cap.
- Two people, always. A 41 m (135 ft) string of their pipe weighs about 34 kg (75 lb); deeper than that they recommend a professional.
- Pipes can drop down the well during assembly; a clamp (their "safety tool") holds the string while the next joint goes on.
- A small weep hole about 1.2 m (4 ft) below the top lets the pump head drain so it doesn't freeze. Air must get in for it to drain: open the check valve's bleeder or disconnect the hose after use.
- With a check valve and gauge it can push water into the house pressure tank: about 45 psi (3.1 bar), never over 50 psi (3.4 bar).

Repairs and frost care are in [Hand and pitcher pumps](#guides/repair_hand_pump).

## A generator for the submersible
A submersible takes far more power to start than to run, and the size you need also depends on the generator's type of voltage regulator. Goulds' minimum generator sizes for 3-wire motors (Goulds IM117):

| Motor | Externally regulated | Internally regulated |
|---|---|---|
| 1/2 hp | 2 kW | 1.5 kW |
| 3/4 hp | 3 kW | 2 kW |
| 1 hp | 4 kW | 2.5 kW |
| 1 1/2 hp | 5 kW | 3 kW |
| 2 hp | 7.5 kW | 4 kW |

These are minimums for typical continuous-duty generators. The table is for 3-wire motors, the kind that need a separate control box (Franklin AIM 60 Hz). A 2-wire motor needs a bigger generator; Franklin's minimums for it are 3 kW for 1/2 hp, 4.5 kW for 3/4 hp, 6 kW for 1 hp and 7.5 kW for 1 1/2 hp (Franklin AIM 60 Hz). Franklin also says the generator must deliver at least 65% of the motor's rated voltage while it starts (Franklin AIM 60 Hz), and Goulds says to ask the generator's maker when in doubt (Goulds IM117). Frequency matters too: running under 60 Hz cuts flow and head, and over 60 Hz can overload the motor (Goulds IM117). Read the pump's voltage on the motor label or control box: the supply has to match the motor's nameplate voltage (Goulds IM117), so a 230 or 240 V pump needs a generator with a 240 V output.

**How it connects.** In Ontario a generator permanently connected to house wiring must go through a transfer device that stops its power flowing back into the grid (ESA generators); ESA allows a portable generator without one only where backfeed is impossible (ESA Flash 25-15-FL). ESA's buying advice names an approved transfer device or switch (ESA generators), and Franklin says manual or automatic transfer switches must be used any time a generator backs up the power lines (Franklin AIM 60 Hz). ESA's diagram for a temporary setup shows a water pump or controller on a plug-in cord run out to the generator (ESA Flash 25-15-FL). In a power cut, treat the pump wiring as live, because the grid can come back (ESA Flash 25-15-FL). Plugging a generator into a wall outlet to feed the house is backfeeding: it can electrocute line workers and neighbours on the same transformer (CPSC 5123). Making that connection is mains-voltage work: see [Isolating mains](#guides/safety_mains_isolation) and [Run a furnace from a generator](#guides/build_furnace_backup_power), and if you haven't done it before, leave the wiring to someone who has.

**Running it.** Start the generator before the pump and stop the pump before the generator (Goulds IM117). Keep the generator outside, at least 6 m (20 ft) from buildings, exhaust away from doors and windows, never in a garage or shed (Health Canada CO). Don't connect it to anything that flood water has reached (ESA Flash 25-15-FL). Fill every tank and tub while it runs.

## A DC pump on solar
Simple Pump sold a 12 V or 24 V motor that drives its hand pump, so the same pump works by hand or by sun; the 12 V motor draws about 10 to 15 A under load (Simple Pump solar kit). Panel sizing and 12 V surface pumps are in [Solar water pump to a raised tank](#guides/build_solar_water_pump).

## Pulling the pump and pipe
Pulling the submersible, to make room for a bucket or to fix it, takes two people at the least.
- Lock off the power first (Simple Pump install). Never lift or hang the pump by its electrical cable (Goulds IM117).
- The check valves hold the water in the drop pipe when the pump stops (Franklin AIM 50 Hz), so you lift a pipe full of water: a 30 mm pipe holds about 0.7 kg per metre (Practica rope pump), so 50 m of it carries about 35 kg of water before you count pipe, cable and pump.
- Alberta recommends a nylon safety rope, tied with a bowline and tightened off at the top of the casing, to limit the fall if a pitless unit or pipe fails (Alberta submersible pumps). If yours has one, keep it tied off while you pull; if not, the pipe is the only thing holding the pump.

## Dug wells
A plain bucket on a rope works in a wide dug well. Keep the cover on between draws: dug-well covers should be strong enough to stand on and childproof, and wood isn't good enough (EFP water wells; Manitoba well fact sheet). Old stone or brick-lined dug wells may be deteriorating and can collapse (EFP water wells).

**Never climb into a well, dug or drilled, or into a well pit.** Gas and oxygen-poor air collect in them (CDC well disinfection; EFP water wells), and people who go in after someone who collapsed die too. Fish things out from the top with a hook or a bucket. See [Confined spaces](#browse/hazards/confined_space).

## Treat what you draw
The cap is one of the barriers that keeps surface water and vermin out (EFP water wells); with it off and a bucket going in and out, assume the water is contaminated. Health Canada's advice for a contaminated well, until tests show it is no longer contaminated, is to bring water to a rolling boil for 1 minute before drinking it or find another safe water source (Health Canada well treatment). A well open to a bucket and rope can pick up contamination, so treat the water the same way. If something got in, see [Shock-chlorinating a well](#guides/skill_shock_chlorinate_well); for testing, see [Testing water](#guides/test_water).
